title: HTML Introduction
summary: What HTML is, how a browser turns it into a page, and how to write and run your very first HTML document.
introduction: Every page on the web, from a personal blog to a banking app, starts as an HTML document. HTML is not a programming language with logic and loops; it is a markup language that labels content so a browser knows what each part is. In this lesson you write a complete page, run it, and learn the three words you will use every day: tag, element and attribute.
learningObjectives: Explain what HTML does and what it does not do
Write a minimal, valid HTML document
Tell tags, elements and attributes apart

blocks.text: HTML stands for **HyperText Markup Language**. *HyperText* means text with links to other documents; *markup* means you wrap pieces of content in labels that describe them. A browser reads those labels and renders the content: a heading becomes large text, a link becomes clickable, an image is fetched and displayed.

HTML works together with two other languages. [CSS](/tutorials/css) controls how things look (colours, layout, spacing) and [JavaScript](/tutorials/javascript) adds behaviour (menus that open, data that loads). HTML comes first because CSS and JavaScript both act on the structure HTML provides.
Create a file called `index.html`, paste the code below, save it and open it in a browser. You now have a working web page.

items: `<!DOCTYPE html>` tells the browser this is a modern HTML document. It must be the first line.
`<html lang="en">` is the root element; `lang` tells browsers and screen readers the page is in English.
`<head>` holds information *about* the page that is not shown in the content area: the character encoding and the title that appears in the browser tab.

rows: The label in angle brackets. Most come in pairs: an opening tag and a closing tag with a slash.
The opening tag, the content and the closing tag together.
Extra information written inside the opening tag as `name="value"`.

blocks.text:
Elements can contain other elements. The `` element contains the `

` elements; we say they are **nested**. Nesting creates a tree, and that tree is what browsers, CSS and JavaScript work with.

HTML cannot make decisions, repeat things or react to clicks on its own. If you need "show this only when the user is logged in", that is JavaScript's job. If you want the heading to be blue, that is CSS. Keeping the three languages in their lanes is what makes websites maintainable.
Forgetting `<!DOCTYPE html>` switches browsers into *quirks mode*, an old compatibility mode where CSS behaves unpredictably. Always start every HTML file with the doctype.
